findings.title: Looking at a broken cabinet counts as damage: powering each cabinet as found to diagnose it scores 6 mistakes (C) and loses the trip bonus
findings.problem: All five cabinets start broken (logic.ts:62-83; the test 'every starting state is broken', logic.test.ts:204-206). The natural way to learn at a repair bench is to switch it on and see what is wrong. Every one of those looks is graded as a mistake. Pinball (across block) trips the fuse and counts a mistake plus a trip (station.ts:288 fault(true)). Rhythm (LED reversed) is dark, so after 0.6 s judge() gives tier 0 and fault(false) counts one (station.ts:390). Claw (220 Ω on 12 V) counts one for the LED over-rating, then another when the block pops (station.ts:300). Handheld (220 Ω on 9 V) counts one for 31.7 mA. Hopper (empty chain) trips again, which is the second trip and loses the 'Fuse tripped no more than once' bonus. My solve.mjs run, which powers every cabinet once as found and then fixes it cleanly, ended with mistakes 6, trips 2 and damage 6 against limits.damage 2 (station.ts:81). That is a C on damage, and the HUD in arcade-teach-22-result.jpg shows 6. The overall grade hides this only because time and cost are A, so the damage axis does not measure understanding. It punishes the observe-then-fix loop the room is built around. The same applies to experiments a learner should be encouraged to make, such as 'what does 100 Ω do?'. Juul's 'fair failure' and DR-02 both say only a mistake in the concept should cost anything, and seeing a fault that was already there is not a mistake. Review4 raised this as A7, and it is still open.
evidence: tests/station-arcade.spec.ts:27-28 (expects mistakes:1 just for pressing POWER on the pinball as found)
solve.mjs log: end mistakes 6, trips 2, damage 6
findings.fix: In station.ts, only count a fault once the setup differs from the cabinet's start. Add a `touched` flag that act() sets on any pick, slot or flip and that showJob() clears. In fault(), return early if !this.touched, so the as-found state is free to observe. Do not count the trip towards `trips` either. Keep counting popped blocks and LEDs, because the player caused those. Raise limits.damage to 3 (the clean spec has 2: the claw pop plus one experiment). Update tests/station-arcade.spec.ts:28 to expect mistakes 0 and trips 0 after the first POWER, and the final `trips` to 0.
findings.verify: Re-run mockups/review5/tools/arcade-teach/solve.mjs. After powering all five cabinets as found and fixing them, snap().station.mistakes should equal only the player-caused pops (1, the claw block) and trips should be 0. tests/station-arcade.spec.ts passes with the updated expectations.
findings.verify_reason: I checked the code and reproduced it. fault() (station.ts:285) runs on the as-found setup with no check that the player changed anything. Pinball: POWER as found gives mistakes 1 and trips 1 (v1 log; spec station-arcade.spec.ts:28 expects exactly this). Claw as found counts 2: the LED over-rating at 0.6 s (mis 4→5 in my log), then the block pop (station.ts:300, mis 5→6). Hopper's empty chain trips, which is trip 2 and loses the 'no more than once' bonus. Damage is added to game.damage (game.ts:353). grade.ts:4 ranks 6 against limit 2 as C. The overall grade is the best of the three parts (grade.ts:6, sort()[0]), so it is hidden, as the finding says. The card's live stars do drop, though: ★★★→★★ in verify-arcade-teach-03, after looking at faults. arcade-teach-22-result.jpg shows damage 6. One claim I could not find: 'Review4 raised this as A7'. There is no A7 in mockups/review4/DESIGN_A.md or DESIGN_B.md.
extra_evidence: src/sim/grade.ts:4-6 (overall = best part, so damage C is hidden)
mockups/review5/shots/verify-arcade-teach-03-pinball-soak-benchview.jpg (card stars already dropped to ★★ after as-found and sweep faults)
mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-teach/v1.mjs log: claw .7 s mis 5, claw 1.8 s mis 6 (popped)
findings.fix_correction: The fix contradicts itself on the claw. With the 'touched' gate, the as-found claw block pop (220 Ω already in the socket) is not player-caused either, yet the verify step expects it to count. Gate popBlock/popLed's mistakes++ and spent+= (station.ts:300, :308) on `touched` too. The as-found claw should cost nothing. The expected end state after a clean observe-then-fix run is then mistakes 0, trips 0. findings.title: Trial and error is free and instant: swapping blocks while live never costs anything, so ★ can be found by sweeping
findings.problem: The bench stays live while the player changes blocks (station.ts:6 'every change shows on the meter at once'). changed() resets runT, explained and faultCounted (station.ts:247), and a tier-0 setup only counts a mistake after it has run 0.6 s (station.ts:390). A pick or slot never adds to `spent`, which is charged only at sign-off (station.ts:273) or when something pops. In fail.mjs I powered 470 Ω, swapped to 100 Ω (29.7 mA, over the LED rating) for 0.3 s, then to 220 Ω. The mistake count did not change. The cheapest strategy is therefore the PhET-slider loop: try 470 (dim, the bar sits left of the band), try 100 (the bar passes the red line), try 220 (★). Nothing asks the player to use I = (V − Vf) ÷ R. The meter shows CHAIN Ω before power but not the voltage left across the chain, so the formula's key term V − Vf never appears as a live number. logic analysis (analyse.mjs) shows how forgiving the search space is. Pinball: the single 220 block is elegant (341 elegant chains of 3375). Claw: 117 elegant. Handheld: 66. Hopper: 186. Only the Rhythm pad (3 elegant, all 47‖47) needs real reasoning. DR-38 asks that brute-force cycling cost credits, and that the elegant tier needs the right margin rather than a lucky value.
findings.fix:
Make prediction the mechanic and let sweeping cost something, without punishing a single experiment.
(1) In act('pick'), charge each block taken from a bin as `this.spent+=BLOCK_COST*.5`. Returning a block (the slot pop branch) refunds nothing, so the cost axis (limits.cost) reflects wasted parts. Recompute limits.cost so a clean run is still an A: sum of best() costs × 1.5.
(2) Add a bonus, 'Called it: three cabinets signed off on the first chain you powered', tracked by a `poweredArrangements` counter per job that increments in act('power') when powered goes true. Add it to the bonuses in station.ts:118-121.
(3) Add a fourth meter tile, 'ACROSS CHAIN  3.0 V' (r.vR when live; before power, show V − Vf in grey as a prediction). Replace or shrink HOTTEST BLOCK, since block heat already has its bar. Put it in drawMeter at station.ts:553-555.
findings.verify: A new spec in tests/station-arcade.spec.ts sweeps 470→100→220 on the pinball. It expects snap().station.spent > 0 before sign-off and the 'Called it' bonus to be unearned. A clean first-try run earns it. Retake arcade-teach-24-crop-meter-playtest.jpg and confirm the ACROSS CHAIN tile.
findings.verify_reason: The DR-38 part is confirmed in code. act('pick') and act('slot') never touch `spent` (station.ts:254-266). Cost is charged only as partsCost of the final setup at sign-off (station.ts:273), so cycling parts is never charged credits, which DR-38's own check forbids. analyse.mjs confirms the bumper is a 4-value sweep: a single 220 is elegant. The claim 'never costs anything' is overstated, though. It only holds at bot speed, as in fail.mjs, which removes and places in the same frame. In my human-timed run (v1.mjs), removing the only block while live left the chain empty: the fuse tripped within 0.15 s, giving mistakes 2 and trips 2. Leaving 100 Ω showing for more than 0.6 s counted another mistake (mis 3). A sweep is free only if the player places the next block in position 2 before removing the first, which I also reproduced (220 via the trick: no new mistake). So sweeping costs damage for a normal player, but never credits. Also, '341 elegant of 3375' counts every permutation of unpacked chains, not distinct designs.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-teach/v1.mjs log: 'removed, empty chain .25s live' gives mis 2, trips 2; '100 placed'+wait gives mis 3; '220 via trick' leaves mis 3 unchanged
findings.fix_correction: (1) is fine. Charging on pick also charges a block that is picked and put straight back (pick toggles `held`, station.ts:255). Charge on slot placement instead (station.ts:264, :259) so that inspecting a bin is free. (3) is fine. Note that the empty-chain trip already penalises the naive swap, so the spec should also cover the series-first swap (place in S, then remove A), which is currently free.

findings.title: The 'PTC fuse' behaves like a bimetal auto-reset breaker: it re-conducts every 2.5 s while powered into the fault, clicks and glows red
findings.problem: Code: the fuse cools while still powered (station.ts:373-374, comment 'cools whether or not the bench is on'), then trips again 0.15 s later (station.ts:376). In fail.mjs I left the pinball's as-found fault powered for 8 s and sampled every 0.25 s. The trace was TTTTTTTTTT.TTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTT., so the fuse cycles about every 2.65 s with a click tone, sparks and the TILT marquee each time. The disc itself goes orange-red with a red halo (arcade-teach-04-pinball-trip.jpg, station.ts:422-425), and the story says 'The fuse keeps clicking' (logic.ts:65). A real polymer PTC (PPTC) does not behave like this. After tripping, a small leakage current keeps it hot and high-resistance for as long as the fault and the voltage remain: it latches. It resets only once the power is removed and it has cooled. Littelfuse says the device stays latched until the fault is cleared and power is removed, and that it needs the low joule-heating leakage current to stay tripped. A PPTC trips at about 125 °C, so it does not glow red, and it makes no sound. The game describes the part as a 'PTC' (logic.ts:13, :28) but gives it a bimetal thermal breaker's behaviour, so a learner gets a false model of a common protection part. Review4 asked for the RESET button to go; this fix went too far the other way.
findings.fix: Keep the name PTC and make it latch. In station.ts:374, count `cooling` down only while !this.powered: `if(this.tripped&&!this.powered){this.cooling-=dt;...}`. While powered and tripped, show a steady 'FUSE TRIPPED: holding' on the meter (station.ts:578), with no repeating click or spark. Change the prompt at station.ts:483 to {key:'P',text:'Power off to reset'}. Replace the red lerp at station.ts:424 with a warm amber tint (#ffb14d, no halo, or halo opacity ≤ 0.25). Story logic.ts:65 becomes 'The fuse keeps tripping.' Update the header comments (logic.ts:13, station.ts:8) to say 'stays tripped while power is on; resets once switched off and cool'. Update tests/station-arcade.spec.ts:31-32: after removing the across block, POWER off, wait 2.6 s, then POWER on.
findings.verify: A new spec: the as-found pinball powered for 6 s has station.tripped===true and the same trip count throughout. After POWER off and 2.6 s, it is untripped. Re-run the fail.mjs PTC trace: it should be all T while powered. Retake arcade-teach-04 and confirm an amber disc.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced. With the as-found pinball left powered for 6 s, the trace was TTTTTTTTTT.TTTTTTTTTTTTT: it re-conducts after about 2.5 s and re-trips 0.15 s later (station.ts:374, :376). The disc is orange-red with a halo in verify-arcade-teach-02-pinball-tripped.jpg, and the prompt reads 'P Fuse cooling' while still powered. A real PPTC latches while the fault and the voltage remain. So the behaviour is a bimetal breaker's, and the comments (logic.ts:13, station.ts:8) describe it as a PTC. Review4 (DESIGN_B.md:31) asked for the self-reset, but the implementation overshoots to cycling-under-fault. I lowered it to P2. The taught concept (a resettable fuse trips on overcurrent, and an across block limits nothing) is correct. The wrong part is the reset behaviour of a secondary component, and mistakes are not re-counted (faultCounted).
extra_evidence: Also in v1: with 100 Ω in place the fuse cooled and re-conducted while powered ('waited for fuse', live:true), without a power cycle

findings.title: A ¼ W block 'pops' within 1.7 s at 1.77× its rating; real resistors are qualified to survive about 6× for 5 s
findings.problem: A block pops as soon as its smoothed heat passes 1.0× its rating (station.ts:383-384, `b.h>1`). With tau 2 s, failTime(1.77) is 1.66 s, and even 1.2× pops in 3.6 s (analyse.mjs). On the claw as found, 220 Ω at 44.8 mA is 441 mW (1.77×). In the capture it glowed at 0.8 s and had popped off the board in a puff of debris by about 2.4 s (arcade-teach-13, -14). The toast reads 'It is a ¼ W part: it popped.' In reality, power ratings are long-term continuous ratings. IEC 60115-1's short-time overload test applies 2.5× rated voltage (6.25× rated power) for 5 s and requires no flashover, burning or breakdown. A ¼ W film resistor at 0.44 W runs very hot (around 200 °C or more), discolours, smells and drifts, and fails over minutes or hours. The game teaches 'over the rating means instant explosion', which conflicts with the gentler, correct LED rule it already uses ('runs hot and dies early', ledPop 2.5×). The Hopper 47 Ω case (1.51×, arcade-teach-34) is about to pop for the same reason.
evidence: src/stations/arcade/logic.test.ts:207-209 ('a part at 150 % of its rating fails after a couple of seconds')
findings.fix:
Add HOUSE.blockPop=2.5 in logic.ts, labelled a house value ('a gross overload; real parts survive brief overloads, but run scorching above their rating').
- station.ts:383: pop only when h>HOUSE.blockPop.
- Between 1× and 2.5×: the block browns, using hotBody's existing lerp toward '#8a4b2a' plus a smoke wisp. judge() already returns tier 0 ('it scorches'); keep that, and change the toast at logic.ts:162 to '…but it is a ¼ W part: it is scorching and will fail.'
- The claw start (220 Ω, 1.77×) then scorches without popping. To keep the claw's 'pop' moment, start it at 100 Ω (3.84×), which pops in about 0.6 s. Note that the LED pops first at 4.9×. Alternatively keep 220 Ω and let it scorch, which is the more truthful lesson.
- Update logic.test.ts:207-209 and the claw part of tests/station-arcade.spec.ts:41-44.
findings.verify: Unit test: a block at 1.5× for 10 s is still on the board (heat ≥ 1, no pop) and the verdict is tier 0 'scorching'. At 3× it pops. Retake arcade-teach-13/14: at 2.4 s the 220 block is browned and smoking, not popped.
findings.verify_reason: Code and run agree. A block pops at heat >1 (station.ts:383). The claw's 220 Ω block at 1.77× popped by 1.8 s in my run, with heat 0.89 at 1.4 s (verify-arcade-teach-08/-09), and analyse.mjs gives failTime 1.66 s. The hopper's 47 Ω at 1.51× also popped (v2 log 'hopper 47 2.6s'). Real ¼ W parts survive short overloads well beyond this, so 'pops off in 2 s at 1.8×' is exaggerated. I lowered it to P2. The direction of the lesson (P = I²R over the rating damages the part) is truthful, and the time compression (HOUSE.tau 2 s) is a labelled house value that fits the physics-comedy rule.
findings.fix_correction: The alternative 'start the claw at 100 Ω to keep a pop' does not work. At 98 mA the LED passes ledPop and pops at 0.5 s, before the block (0.6 s), so the claw's pop moment becomes the LED's, not the block's. With blockPop 2.5×, no single-block claw start gives a block pop without the LED popping or the fuse tripping first (47 Ω trips at 206 mA). Adopt the 'keep 220 Ω and let it scorch' option: brown plus smoke, with judge's existing 'it scorches' wording. Optionally add a slow failure (pop after about 8 s above 1×) so the consequence still lands in the world.

findings.title: An LED at 21 mA is a FAIL: the 20 mA test current is treated as an absolute maximum
findings.problem: led() sets imax 0.02 (logic.ts:60), and judge() makes anything above it tier 0, 'over the LED's 20 mA rating: it runs hot and dies early' (logic.ts:158). The claw with a single 470 Ω block gives 21.0 mA (5 % over) and Fails, with the play test blocked (analyse.mjs: claw single 470 '21.0mA t0'). The meter draws the LED's red limit line at exactly 20 mA (station.ts:569). Typical 5 mm LED datasheets characterise at IF = 20 mA but rate the continuous forward current at 30 mA (for example Waitrony W05310YUC: continuous 30 mA, measured at 20 mA), and Cree recommends 10–30 mA. The game teaches '20 mA is a cliff', the most widespread LED misconception, and the 'dies early' wording does not match a 5 % margin. It also makes the claw's 470 Ω answer fail for a reason a real tech would call fine-but-warm.
findings.fix:
Give Led two numbers in logic.ts: `inom:.02` ('rated, the datasheet test current') and `imax:.03` ('absolute maximum').
- judge(): tier 0 only above imax (30 mA).
- 20–30 mA becomes tier 1 with the note '24 mA is above the LED's 20 mA rated current: it runs warm and wears out sooner.'
- Keep the band top at 20 mA so reliable or elegant still means at or below rated.
- ledPop becomes 2.5× of inom (50 mA). Unchanged.
- Meter: draw a dashed amber line at inom and a solid red line at imax on the LIGHT bar (station.ts:569).
- Update logic.test.ts:182 (the claw 100 Ω case is still tier 0 at 98 mA).
findings.verify: logic.test: claw 470 alone is tier 1 with a 'rated current' note, and bumper 100 Ω (29.7 mA) is tier 1. Retake arcade-teach-24-crop-meter-playtest.jpg and confirm the two limit lines.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced. The claw with a single 470 Ω block reads 21.02 mA, tier 0, toast '21.0 mA is over the LED's 20 mA rating: it runs hot and dies early'. It counts a mistake (mis 6→7) and the soak never starts (v1 log 'claw single 470'). imax .02 (logic.ts:60) is used as the hard fail line (logic.ts:158). Typical 5 mm LEDs are tested at 20 mA and rated about 25–30 mA continuous, so failing a 5 % overshoot with 'dies early' teaches a cliff. I set P2 rather than P1: the band and its ★ zone still steer players to 10–15 mA, and the error is in where the fail line sits, not in the formula.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-teach/v1.mjs log 'claw single 470': iL 21.02, mis 7, soak 0, toast '...dies early'

findings.title: LED HEAT shows °C values that teach a wrong number: the 'limit' line sits at 45 °C and LEDs pop at about 43 °C
findings.problem: The LED HEAT bar plots m.led (a current ratio) against a red line at 1 and labels it in °C as 25 + m.led·500·imax·vf (station.ts:570). For a red LED the line falls at 45 °C. In arcade-teach-30 the 47 Ω pinball LED shows 43 °C and then pops at 0.7 s (arcade-teach-31). The pop is driven by the instantaneous r.level > 2.5 (station.ts:386), not by the heat the bar shows, so the bar has not crossed its own line when the LED dies. The failure therefore does not show its cause on the instrument meant to show it (DR-28). The number is also misleading in itself: 5 mm LEDs are specified to operate up to 65–95 °C ambient, with junction limits around 100–125 °C, and 45 °C is a warm, perfectly healthy LED. A learner reading the bench leaves believing LEDs fail at 45 °C. The handheld at 31.7 mA ('runs hot') shows only 46 °C (arcade-teach-16).
findings.fix:
Either:
(a) Drop °C from LED HEAT. Label the bar 'LED LOAD' with right-hand text like '1.6× rated'. Draw the pop threshold (2.5×) as a skull tick and the rated (1×) as a dashed line, using the instantaneous r.level for the bar, so a pop is always visible as the bar sitting past the skull tick.
Or:
(b) Keep °C with honest values. Junction = 25 + θ·I·Vf with θ = 500, and mark the abs-max junction at 100 °C. Pop when the smoothed junction temperature exceeds 125 °C, which with θ 500 is about 100 mA for red. That needs ledPop re-derived from temperature, so `popLed` triggers from heat.led and the bar always crosses its line first.
Option (a) is simpler. Change station.ts:570 and drawMeter's bar() call, and gate popLed on the same value the bar shows.
findings.verify: Retake arcade-teach-30 (47 Ω pinball, 0.4 s). The LED bar sits beyond its pop tick before the pop frame (arcade-teach-31), and no °C under 100 is labelled as a limit.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced from cold with 47 Ω on the pinball. heat.led was 0.69 at 0.5 s (≈39 °C on the bar, below its red line at 45 °C) when the LED popped at about 0.55 s (v2 log; verify-arcade-teach-16 shows 'LED HEAT 39 °C' under the line one frame before the pop). The pop is driven by instantaneous r.level>2.5 for 0.5 s (station.ts:386), not by the bar (station.ts:570). The bar crosses the line only if the LED was already warm (my warm run: 1.01 at 0.3 s). The °C limit of 45 °C is misleading. I lowered it to P2: the LIGHT bar right above does sit pinned past its red rating line, so the cause is visible on the meter, just not on the bar labelled HEAT.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/shots/verify-arcade-teach-16-led47-cold-0_5s.jpg (LED HEAT 39 °C below the line; LIGHT bar past it)

findings.title: Coin hopper: the meter says MOTOR FULL and PLAY TEST PASSED ✓ while the verdict says 'too dim'; the ★ zone rewards the least base overdrive
findings.problem: For the base job, the MOTOR bar shows FULL as soon as Ib·β ≥ 200 mA, which is Ib ≥ 2 mA with β 100 (station.ts:571, :410-411). The band, though, is 4–10 mA (logic.ts:79). With 470+470+470 Ω (3.05 mA) the meter shows MOTOR FULL and PLAY TEST PASSED ✓. The toast says 'Works: 3.05 mA is under the 4–10 mA band: too dim.' (arcade-teach-35, -36; logic.ts:167 uses 'too dim' for every load, including a motor). The player sees a motor at full speed, a passing kid and a sentence about brightness. Nothing shows why 4 mA matters. The physics: a switching BJT is driven with a forced β of about 10–20 (Ib ≈ Ic/10), because β varies between parts and falls at high current. Driving Ib = Ic/β_typ (2 mA) leaves it on the edge of saturation, hot and slow. The ★ zone is 'the lowest third of the band' (logic.ts:140), 4–6 mA, which is forced β 33–50, and the note 'a little more resistance wastes less power' (logic.ts:171) rewards the riskiest drive. For an LED, less current is good practice. For a saturated switch, the opposite is true, and the game teaches the LED rule on a transistor. The story's 'The motor needs 2 mA of base current' (logic.ts:81) makes the same point the wrong way round.
findings.fix:
In logic.ts:
- Give Base a `betaMin:40` (worst-case part at 200 mA) next to beta 100.
- Story: 'A typical transistor needs 2 mA of base current to pass the motor's 200 mA, but a weak one needs 5.'
- Band [.005,.015].
- starZone: for base loads, take the middle third (8.3–11.7 mA) and drop the 'wastes less power' note. Replace it with 'Plenty of drive: even a weak transistor switches fully on.'
- logic.ts:167: use `isLed?'too dim':'the transistor is only half on'`.

In station.ts:410-411 and :571, show two MOTOR states:
- 'FULL' only when Ib·betaMin ≥ motor;
- between Ib·beta ≥ motor and that, a 'FULL (typical part only)' amber state, with the motor wheel juddering.

Check best(hopper) still exists: 470 alone gives 9.1 mA, so it does. Update logic.test.ts:198-203 and tests/station-arcade.spec.ts:53-55.
findings.verify: logic.test: hopper 470×3 (3.05 mA) gives tier 0 or tier 1 with 'half on', and the elegant chain gives 8–12 mA. Retake arcade-teach-35: the motor bar is amber and juddering, not FULL, whenever the toast says under band.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced with 470+470+470 on the hopper (3.05 mA). The meter shows MOTOR FULL in mint and PLAY TEST PASSED ✓. The toast says 'Works: 3.05 mA is under the 4–10 mA band: too dim.' (verify-arcade-teach-11-hopper-1410.jpg). Drive = Ib·β/motor reaches 1 at 2 mA (station.ts:410, :571), while the band starts at 4 mA (logic.ts:79). 'too dim' is used for every load (logic.ts:167). starZone is the lowest third for every load (logic.ts:140), so the ★ zone for a saturated switch rewards the least overdrive. That is the LED rule applied to a transistor. Three signals contradict each other on the room's only transistor job.

findings.title: The transistor's job, a small base current switching a big motor current, is never drawn: no collector, no motor circuit on the board
findings.problem: For the coin hopper, drawBoard() prints only 'B' and 'E' at the TO-92 (station.ts:527). The board shows logic pin → fuse → chain → base → emitter → ground. The motor is a grey can with a coin wheel parked beside the meter (station.ts:178-180), with no lead from it to the transistor's collector and no motor supply (arcade-teach-21, -34). The defining idea of the job, that milliamps into the base control 200 mA through collector–emitter from a separate supply, exists only in the story sentence and in a MOTOR bar. A player who solves it learns 'put about 900 Ω before the black thing'. That is the same lesson as the LED cabinets with a different target number. Nothing shows amplification or switching.
findings.fix:
When j.load.kind==='base', drawBoard() draws a second loop:
- a '12 V MOTOR' post at the right edge;
- a thick trace to the motor (move the motor group to board coordinates around (ACRX, TOPZ−.05)), then on to the transistor's 'C' leg, with 'E' going to ground. Add a 'C' text label at LEDX+.1, TOPZ.
- Make that trace twice as wide (lineWidth 28 vs 16), so 200 mA reads as the bigger current.
- In animate(), pulse the thick trace's emissive with `drive`. This is a moving-dash texture offset proportional to the current: base-loop dashes slow, motor-loop dashes fast, appearing only on a closed live loop (DR-29).
- Hide the ACROSS slot for this job (it has no meaning on a base).
findings.verify: Retake the hopper bench shot (arcade-teach-21) with the HUD hidden. A first-time viewer can trace two loops, a thin one through the chain and a thick one through the motor, and the motor loop animates only when the base current is on.
findings.verify_reason: Looked at it. drawBoard prints only 'B' and 'E' at the TO-92 (station.ts:527). The traces are the same LED rails (station.ts:518-521). The motor is a grey can parked behind the board beside the meter (station.ts:178, at top-local (1.1, -.46)) with no lead to the transistor and no motor supply (verify-arcade-teach-11 and -13). Nothing on the board shows a small base current switching a separate large current. The room's distinct transistor idea exists only in the panel story text.

findings.title: The prompt says 'P  Play test' during the play test, but P switches the bench off and wipes the test
findings.problem: prompt(): `if(this.powered)return {key:'P',text:this.soak>0?'Play test':'Power off'}` (station.ts:484). While the kid is playing, the pill reads 'P Play test' (arcade-teach-06-pinball-playtest.jpg), which looks like an instruction to press P to play-test. Pressing it calls powerOff() → changed(), which sets soak to 0 and powered to false. In fail.mjs, mid-test at soak 1.5, KeyP gave powered:false and soak:0, and the prompt flipped to 'P Power on'. A player following the HUD cancels the success they just earned and has to wait again. This is exactly what DR-19 forbids: a key prompt whose key does the opposite of its label, during a moment the player is trying to complete.
evidence: fail.mjs log: 'mid playtest … soak 1.5' → 'after pressing P … pw:false, soak:0'
findings.fix: station.ts:484: while soak>0 && !soakDone, return a non-key status: {key:'',text:'Kid is play-testing…'}. If the Prompt type requires a key, use {key:'⏳',text:'Play-testing…'} and make game-ui render a keyless pill. Otherwise return 'P Power off'. Consider also ignoring P for 0.3 s after the test starts.
findings.verify: Capture during the play test: the prompt pill shows no P. A spec presses P mid-test only when the prompt says 'Power off'. A new assertion in tests/station-arcade.spec.ts checks the prompt text during the soak does not contain 'P'.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced. With the mouse off all clickables, the pill reads 'P Play test' during the soak (verify-arcade-teach-03-pinball-soak-benchview.jpg; station.ts:484). Pressing KeyP mid-soak (soak 1.6) gave powered false, soak 0, and the prompt 'P Power on' (v1 log 'pressed P mid soak'). A player who obeys the pill cancels the test they were completing, which breaks DR-19. It is not a soft-lock, so P1 rather than P0.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-teach/v1.mjs log 'mid soak' prompt 'PPlay test', then 'pressed P mid soak' pw:false soak:0

findings.title: Failure effects hide the taught part: a 400 px smoke ball covers the LED and the meter, and the overdriven LED's halo floods the chain
findings.problem:
The pop moments are the room's best 'show why' beats, but the effects cover what they should be showing.
- In arcade-teach-31-led-popped.jpg, the LED pop's smoke burst (station.ts:311, 10 'smoke' particles) makes a pale disc about 400 px wide over the LED, the right half of the board and two-thirds of the meter at the very moment the meter's numbers explain the failure.
- In arcade-teach-14-claw-popped.jpg, the block pop's smoke (station.ts:303) covers the whole meter screen.
- In arcade-teach-13-claw-hot-1_4s.jpg, the overdriven green LED's halo sprite (ledHalo, scale 0.4 + glowK·0.8, opacity up to 0.95, station.ts:408) washes the whole board green. The hot 220 Ω block, the part being taught (P = I²R), can hardly be seen under it, and the pre-pop smoke puffs (station.ts:420-421) drift over the meter.
- In arcade-teach-16/-30, the red halo floods the chain socket and the ACROSS slot.
DR-66 caps glow sprites at opacity ≤ 0.5 and 1.5× their source, and says they must never hide the part being taught. DR-79 says effects never block the taught part for more than 0.3 s.
findings.fix:
station.ts:408: clamp the halo to `opacity=Math.min(.5,glowK*.4)` and `scale=.3+Math.min(1.6,glowK)*.25` (at most about 0.7 m). Show the overdrive with a flickering dome and a pulsing rim ring instead.

For both pop bursts (lines 303 and 311), use 3–4 small smoke puffs, at most 0.08 m each, rising and drifting toward −z (away from the camera, behind the meter's lower edge). Fade each in 0.6 s.

At pop time, also freeze the meter frame for 1.5 s showing the fatal reading, e.g. 'LED: 62.5 mA = 3.1× rated → POPPED' in red. Then the cause stays readable after the smoke.
findings.verify: Retake arcade-teach-13, -14, -30 and -31. The meter and the chain socket stay legible in every frame. The halo crop has opacity ≤ 0.5 (median luma change ≤ 40 over the chain pads).
findings.verify_reason: Seen in my own shots. The LED pop smoke is a large pale disc over the right half of the board and most of the meter (verify-arcade-teach-06-led47-popped.jpg). The block-pop smoke covers the meter (verify-arcade-teach-09-claw-1_8s.jpg). The overdriven green halo washes the board green (-08), and the red halo floods the S/D pads and the ACROSS slot (-16). ledHalo opacity reaches 0.95 (station.ts:408), above DR-66's 0.5 cap. Two parts are overstated. The hot 220 Ω block is still clearly visible and orange in -08, not 'hardly seen'. DR-79 caps effects blocking Pip at 0.3 s; it says nothing about the taught part (DR-66 is the rule that covers the taught part). The toast still states the cause, so the smoke is polish, not P1.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/RULES.md DR-79 wording ('never block Pip'), DR-66 ('never hide ... the part being taught')

findings.title: The play-test kid, the room's only 'it works' character beat, is off-screen in the bench view
findings.problem: The success loop is 'a kid plays the cabinet while it runs in spec' (station.ts:7, :225-232, :427-431). The kid hops, mashes buttons and cheers with arms up when the test passes, and slumps at a dark screen. The serviced cabinet and the kid stand at the bench's left end, t.x+OX−2.75 (station.ts:215). The bench camera (view distance 5.9, pitch 0.98, station.ts:80) frames only the bench. In arcade-teach-06/-07 (play test running and passed) only a sliver of the pink cabinet shows at the left edge, and no kid. They appear only after standing up with Esc (arcade-teach-32, -33). So the reward reaches the player as a purple progress bar and the text 'PLAY TEST PASSED ✓'. The cabinet's marquee lamp and screen, which react to the LED (station.ts:409, :426), are out of frame too, and so is the slump on failure. This loses the in-world consequence DR-28 and DR-47 call for, and the fun beat DR-11 asks for.
findings.fix:
Move the serviced cabinet into the bench frame. Either place it behind the bins at the bench's back-left, at about group(game.root, t.x+OX−1.6, 0, t.z−1.25, .25) with the kid facing it at +z, so the marquee, screen and kid sit above the bins in the station view. Or widen the view (distance 6.6, lookY .45, a little left) so the existing cabinet fits.

Move its solid() colliders to match, and check the cabinet doesn't hide the meter.

Keep the purple soak bar, but make the kid's cheer the main signal, with a speech bubble 'Again!' at soakDone.
findings.verify: Retake arcade-teach-06 and -07 from the bench view. The kid, cabinet screen and marquee are inside the frame, the kid visibly hops during the soak and raises both arms at PASS, and the meter is not occluded.
findings.verify_reason: In the bench view during the soak, only a pink sliver of the cabinet shows at the left edge, with no kid, screen or marquee (verify-arcade-teach-03-pinball-soak-benchview.jpg). The kid and the PRIZES cabinet appear left of the bench only after standing up (verify-arcade-teach-14-stood-up-soak.jpg). The cabinet group sits at t.x+OX−2.75 (station.ts:215), beyond the bench's left end (bench W 4.3, so the edge is at cx−2.15), and the bench camera is distance 5.9 (station.ts:80). The hop/cheer/slump animation (station.ts:427-431) plays entirely out of frame, so the success beat reaches the player as a bar and a line of text.

findings.title: Rhythm pad (blue LED on 3.3 V) teaches false precision: with 0.3 V of headroom, real Vf and supply spread swing the current from 0 to 27 mA
findings.problem: The Rhythm pad is the only cabinet that really needs reasoning (one elegant answer, 47‖47 = 23.5 Ω; analyse.mjs), so it is the room's 'apply the idea' moment. It rests on Vf being exactly 3.0 V on an exact 3.3 V rail (logic.ts:59, :67-70). Sweeping blue Vf from 2.8 to 3.2 V and the rail ±5 % (3.135–3.465 V) with the intended 47‖47 gives anywhere from 0.0 to 27.1 mA (analyse.mjs). Real blue LEDs span roughly 2.8–3.6 V, and practitioners say a series resistor cannot regulate a blue LED on 3.3 V: use 5 V or a constant-current driver. The game grades this as 'Elegant ★' and teaches that a 0.3 V headroom design is ideal, which is the opposite of the real lesson. The story line 'Only 0.3 V is left over' (logic.ts:69) states the key fact but frames it as a puzzle detail, not a warning. The bumper's design (3 V of headroom) is barely affected by the same Vf spread (14.5/13.6/12.7 mA), which is the contrast worth teaching.
findings.fix:
Keep the parallel puzzle and make it honest.
- In judge() (logic.ts:170-172), cap the tier at 2 when V − Vf < 0.8 V, with the note 'Works, but with only 0.3 V spare, a slightly different LED or a sagging supply swings the current a lot. Real designs leave more headroom or use a current driver.'
- Or move the Rhythm pad to 5 V with a white LED (Vf 3.0) and band 12–20 mA. Then 47‖47 + 47 + 47 = 117.5 Ω gives 16.9 mA, and parallel is still needed. Re-check with best().
- Optionally add a 'TOLERANCE' toggle on the meter that ghosts the LIGHT bar at Vf ± 0.2 V, so headroom becomes visible.
- Update logic.test.ts:172-176 and tests/station-arcade.spec.ts:36-40.
findings.verify: logic.test: the rhythm 47‖47 verdict carries the headroom note (or the new 5 V job's best() needs a side-by-side pair). Retake arcade-teach-11.
findings.verify_reason: The arithmetic checks out. 47‖47 + 1 Ω wire = 24.5 Ω. At the nominal 3.0 V / 3.3 V that is 12.2 mA (my run: 12.24 mA, tier 3). analyse.mjs gives 27.1 mA at Vf 2.8 / 3.465 V and 0 mA at Vf 3.2 / 3.135 V. Grading a 0.3 V-headroom design as Elegant ★ does miss the real lesson. I lowered it to P2. The model's fixed Vf is an explicitly labelled simplification (logic.ts:15-17, panel profile station.ts:455), so the room is truthful at the level it says it teaches. This is an enrichment, not a false statement.

findings.title: No visible consequence when the logic pin is overloaded: motor FULL, lamp lit, only a sentence and a formula
findings.problem: Hopper with a single 47 Ω block gives 89.6 mA from a pin rated 20 mA. judge() fails it with '89.6 mA is over the logic pin's 20 mA rating. (I = (5 V − 0.7 V) ÷ R)' (logic.ts:159). In the world (arcade-teach-34), the MOTOR bar reads FULL in mint, the coin wheel spins, the cabinet lamp lights (drive ≥ 1, station.ts:410-411), and only the BASE bar passes its red line. The 'LOGIC PIN' supply is a plain brass post (station.ts:150), with no chip to warm, smoke or brown out. The visible cue praises the fault, and the cause exists only as text plus a formula, which is method, not cause (DR-28; review4 A8). The empty-chain case says the junction 'draws amps' (logic.ts:151). A 5 V logic pin cannot source amps: its output resistance (tens of ohms) limits it to roughly 60–150 mA, above an ATmega328P's 40 mA absolute maximum.
findings.fix:
Replace the SUPPLY post for base jobs with a small black 'logic chip' rbox(.18,.04,.12) with 8 legs.
- Add a heat value: hotBody-style lerp to orange and a smoke wisp when iLoad > imax.
- Above 2× imax, the pin 'browns out': drive drops to 0, the motor stops, and the chip's status dot goes red.
- Model the pin with a 40 Ω output resistance (HOUSE.pinR) in read() for base jobs, so the empty chain gives (5 − 0.7) / 41 ≈ 105 mA. That still trips the 100 mA fuse, or remove the fuse from the base channel.
- logic.ts:151 base text: 'Nothing in the chain limits the current: the pin tries to push about 100 mA, five times its 20 mA rating.'
- Drop the formula from logic.ts:158-159 and show it live as the meter's ACROSS CHAIN tile instead (see the trial-and-error finding).
findings.verify: Retake arcade-teach-34 with the HUD hidden. The chip glows orange and smokes, the motor stalls, and a first-time viewer names 'the chip is overloaded' without the toast.
findings.verify_reason: Partly corrected. Hopper with a single 47 Ω block: MOTOR FULL in mint, and only the BASE bar passes its red line (verify-arcade-teach-13-hopper-47.jpg). The LOGIC PIN is a plain brass post (station.ts:150). The overloaded pin has no device-level consequence. The claim 'no visible consequence' is wrong, though. The 47 Ω block runs at 1.51× its rating, glows orange (BLOCK HEAT 110 °C in -13), smokes and pops off at about 2.2 s, with a toast about the block's heat (v2 log 'hopper 47 2.6s'). So the in-world consequence lands on the wrong part and the explanation switches from 'pin rating' to 'block popped'. That misattribution is the real teaching problem. The cabinet lamp is off-screen in the bench view, so 'lamp lit' is not something the player sees there. 'draws amps' (logic.ts:151) is confirmed.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-teach/v2.mjs log 'hopper 47 2.6s': toast 'The 47 Ω block turned 377 mW into heat ... it popped.'
findings.fix_correction: Also cover the misattributed pop. Either keep a base-job block from popping while the pin is the limiting fault: check `r.iLoad>j.load.imax` before popBlock for base loads. Or make the pin/chip brown out first (drive→0), so the pin, not the block, is the visible failure. With HOUSE.pinR 40 Ω, recheck best(hopper) and the rush generator, because read() changes.

findings.title: Popped-LED toast says 'it runs hot and dies early', the wrong cause for an LED that just died outright
findings.problem: popLed() shows judge().problems[0] (station.ts:307-309), which for any over-rating LED is '… over the LED's 20 mA rating: it runs hot and dies early. (I = (V − Vf) ÷ R)' (logic.ts:158). The 47 Ω pinball LED at 62.5 mA (3.1×) vanishes in a flash and smoke (arcade-teach-31), but the toast describes slow wear. The fallback 'The LED ran far past its rating and popped.' (station.ts:309) is never reached because problems[0] always exists. The single cause sentence (DR-28) contradicts the event on screen, and the player cannot tell the gross-overload rule (ledPop 2.5×) from the 'runs hot' rule, the distinction review4 asked for.
evidence: fail.mjs log '47 popped … toast: 62.5 mA is over the LED's 20 mA rating: it runs hot and dies early'
findings.fix: station.ts:309: always say `${mA(r.iLoad)} mA is ${(r.level).toFixed(1)}× the LED's rating: far too much, it burned out at once. A spare goes in.` Keep judge()'s 'runs hot and dies early' for the 1–2.5× band only.
findings.verify: Re-run fail.mjs step 4: the toast after the pop contains 'burned out'.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced. After the 47 Ω pinball LED popped, the toast read '62.5 mA is over the LED's 20 mA rating: it runs hot and dies early. (I = (V − Vf) ÷ R)' (verify-arcade-teach-06; v2 log '47 cold .65'). popLed uses judge().problems[0] (station.ts:307-309). For any level > 2.5 that is always the over-rating sentence, so the fallback on :309 is unreachable. The cause sentence describes slow wear right after an instant failure.

findings.title: An overdriven LED flashes white and the story calls it 'white-hot': incandescent imagery that teaches the wrong overload cue
findings.problem: animate() lerps the LED dome colour up to 70 % toward #ffffff once heat.led > 0.9 (station.ts:407). The red and green LEDs in arcade-teach-13/-16/-30 read as white domes with coloured halos. The claw story says 'The claw light glows white-hot' (logic.ts:73). An LED's colour comes from its semiconductor bandgap, not from temperature, so an overdriven red LED is a brighter red (slightly red-shifted as it heats). It never turns white. White-hot is a filament or resistor-wire image. Players who later see a white LED may read it as 'overloaded'. Separately, an unlit red LED is drawn 55 % toward white (station.ts:501, tint()), so the pinball's red LED looks white at rest (arcade-teach-03), which blurs the colour lesson (the different Vf per colour) further.
findings.fix:
station.ts:407: when over, keep the hue and show the overload as saturation clipping plus a 12 Hz flicker of the halo, a hot-orange rim ring and a heat-shimmer wisp. No white lerp.
- tint(): lerp the unlit dome 0.25 toward white (not 0.55) and keep the hue visible.
- logic.ts:73: 'The claw light glares far too bright and its block smells hot.'
- logic.ts:15 header: add 'LED colour does not change with current.'
findings.verify: Retake arcade-teach-03, -13 and -30. The unlit pinball LED reads pink-red, and the overdriven LEDs keep their hue.
findings.verify_reason: The overdriven green claw LED renders as a white dome (verify-arcade-teach-08-claw-1_4s.jpg) through the white lerp at station.ts:407, and the story says 'glows white-hot' (logic.ts:73). The unlit red pinball LED is a pale pink-white disc (verify-arcade-teach-15-crop-led-unlit-red.jpg; tint() 0.55 toward white, station.ts:501). Both are real colour-cue problems.

findings.title: 'PLAY TEST PASSED ✓' and sign-off for out-of-band setups contradicts the card's ask and the 'too dim' note
findings.problem: Any tier ≥ 1 setup soaks and passes (station.ts:391-392). The Rhythm pad with one 47 Ω block (6.25 mA, band 10–20) shows a green 'PLAY TEST PASSED ✓', a lit sign-off button and the toast 'Works: 6.25 mA is under the 10–20 mA band: too dim.' (arcade-teach-10). The job card step reads 'Rhythm pad: Blue LED on 3.3 V: 10–20 mA' (station.ts:117), but signing off at 6 mA ticks it anyway. A first-time player gets three messages at once: passed, too dim, and a requirement that did not apply. The tiers are a reasonable Zachtronics-style 'solved, then metrics' design, but the copy needs to say so. The card text also has a double colon ('Pinball bumper: Red LED on 5 V: 12–20 mA'), and the same ask appears on both the card and the panel h4 (DR-41).
findings.fix:
For tier 1, set the soak strip to amber with 'PLAYS · DIM' or 'PLAYS · OVER BAND' (station.ts:577) instead of green PASSED, and have the kid shrug, not cheer.
- Card step text: `${j.title} — ${j.ask.replace(':',' ·')}` to remove the double colon.
- Drop the h4 ask from the panel when the card already shows it (station.ts:449), keeping one copy (DR-41).
findings.verify: Retake arcade-teach-10. The strip is amber, the kid shrugs, and the ask appears once on screen.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced. Rhythm with one 47 Ω block (6.25 mA) passes the soak: verdict tier 1, prompt 'Enter Sign off', toast 'Works: 6.25 mA is under the 10–20 mA band: too dim.' (v1 log 'rhythm 47 alone'; verify-arcade-teach-07). The double colon shows on the card ('Pinball bumper: Red LED on 5 V: 12–20 mA'). The same ask also appears in the panel h4 (verify-arcade-teach-01/-03). A further stale-text case: the previous arrangement's fail toast ('29.7 mA is over the LED's 20 mA rating…') was still up during the passing 220 Ω play test (verify-arcade-teach-03), adding to the mixed signals.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/shots/verify-arcade-teach-03-pinball-soak-benchview.jpg (card and h4 duplicate the ask; stale fail toast during a passing test)
src/stations/arcade/station.ts:437 (toast lives max(4, len·0.06) s and is not cleared by changed())

findings.title: Stale hover prompt: 'F  Flip the LED' shows during the coin-hopper job, which has no LED
findings.problem: hoverHint() returns the hovered clickable's action (station.ts:457-466). hovered is only updated on pointer events (station.ts:344-350). When showJob() hides the LED group for the base job (station.ts:242), the stale hover stays, so the prompt pill reads 'F Flip the LED' through the whole hopper job (arcade-teach-19, -21, -35). The LED group also stays scaled to 1.08. act('flip') returns false for base loads (station.ts:267), so the key does nothing: a false prompt (DR-19). The same stale hover replaced the 'Enter Sign off' prompt on the handheld after its pass (solve.mjs log 'handheld fixed … prompt: F Flip the LED'), which hides the next real action.
findings.fix:
In showJob() and redraw(), clear the hover when the hovered object is no longer visible: `if(this.hovered&&!visibleUp(this.hovered.obj)){this.hovered.obj.scale.copy(this.hovered.obj.userData.baseScale);this.hovered=undefined;}`.

In prompt(), put soakDone ('Enter Sign off') before hoverHint, so the next real step always wins (swap lines 480-481).
findings.verify: Re-run solve.mjs. During the hopper the prompt never reads 'Flip the LED', and after any pass it reads 'Enter Sign off'.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced. I rested the mouse on the LED and used only act/keys. At the hopper (LED hidden) the prompt was still 'F Flip the LED'. It switched to '1–4 Take a block' only after the mouse moved (v2 log 'hopper start, mouse unmoved' / 'after mouse move'; verify-arcade-teach-17). hovered is refreshed only in pointer() (station.ts:344-347). Also confirmed: with the soak done, a hover on the LED gave 'F Flip the LED' instead of 'Enter Sign off', because hoverHint is checked before soakDone (station.ts:480-481). This is P2 because any mouse movement clears it.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-teach/v2.mjs log 'hover led, soak done' prompt 'FFlip the LED' with done:true

findings.title: Rhythm pad introduces three new ideas at once (polarity, parallel, low headroom); the ladder has no reuse step
findings.problem:
Job order (logic.ts:62-83):
1. Series limiting plus the across trap.
2. Polarity (flip), parallel (side by side, the only way to reach the band) and the 0.3 V headroom idea.
3. Power rating (P = I²R) plus series chaining.
4. Battery life.
5. A transistor base.

Cabinet 2 piles on polarity, parallel and headroom, and the next cabinet never asks for parallel again (best() for claw, handheld and hopper is 470+470 in series). So 'side by side' is used once and dropped. Polarity is never revisited either. DR-27 asks for one new idea per job, reusing the previous one.
findings.fix:
Split the ideas over the jobs:
- 2 Rhythm: reversed only, with a working single-block chain. That is polarity alone.
- 3 Claw: 220 Ω start, power rating, needs about 1 kΩ in series.
- 4 Handheld: battery, the lowest current that is still visible.
- 5 Hopper.
- Add a 6th or replace one: 'Light gun' with a white LED on 5 V, where the bins lack a small enough single value, so a side-by-side pair is required and must reuse polarity (it starts reversed).
Check each with best() and judge(start) < 2 in logic.test.ts:204.
findings.verify: A table of new and reused ideas per job in logic.test.ts comments. best() for the parallel job contains a two-block position. Retake bench shots per job.
findings.verify_reason: In logic.ts:62-83, analyse.mjs ('best' per job) and the spec (station-arcade.spec.ts:36-55), only the rhythm pad starts reversed and needs a side-by-side pair (best [[47,47]]). Claw, handheld and hopper all solve with 470+470 in series. Neither polarity nor parallel is reused, which goes against DR-27's 'add one idea, reuse the previous one'. The headroom point is the reason parallel is needed rather than a separate mechanic, so it is really two new ideas in job 2, not three.

notes.teaching:
What works: the arcade has the truest and most mechanical teaching of the station rooms. The chain socket makes series and parallel a physical act: blocks end to end add, and side by side they share, joined by brass bus bars. The board's printed traces make the ACROSS slot read as a parallel path. The 'across limits nothing' trap fails at once with a correct, cause-first sentence. The maths in read() is right: I = (V − Vf)/R_total with 1 Ω of wiring, the current split in a pair, the resistor across the LED carrying vf/rp, and battery life = mAh/I. The Rhythm pad is the one cabinet where the player has to apply an idea (no single block works, so they have to try side by side). The pinball's 220 Ω answer is the textbook one.

Where it falls short:
- Tuning and truth. The PTC behaves like a bimetal breaker. Blocks pop at 1.77× within 1.7 s, although real resistors are qualified to take 6.25× for 5 s. 20 mA is treated as a cliff, although 5 mm LEDs are rated for 30 mA continuous. LED HEAT shows a 45 °C 'limit'. The Rhythm design rests on 0.3 V of headroom, which real Vf spread breaks.
- The transistor job. It looks like the LED jobs with a different target number. The collector and motor circuit are never drawn, the meter says MOTOR FULL and PASSED while the verdict says 'too dim', and the ★ zone rewards the least overdrive, which is the opposite of good switch design.
- Learning by trial and error. The bench is live while blocks change, sweeping is free (fail.mjs: 470→100→220 in 0.3 s steps cost nothing), and four of five cabinets have dozens to hundreds of elegant chains. A player can win by watching the bar rather than using V − Vf, and the meter never shows V − Vf as a live number.
- Grading. Simply observing the broken cabinets as found scores 6 mistakes.
notes.fun: The juice is good when you can see it. The fuse sparks, the marquee shows TILT!, a popped block sprays candy debris across the bench and floor (arcade-teach-14), and the kid's arms go up on a pass (arcade-teach-33). But that kid and the serviced cabinet are outside the bench camera, so the main reward reaches a seated player as a purple progress bar. The smoke and halo effects also cover the board and meter in the most dramatic frames. The room still has no designed chaos shortcut, and the cable is absent (DR-01, DR-05, both known). The 3 s play test does not drag: the five play tests total about 15 s. Pressing P during the test, which the prompt invites, cancels it, which makes it feel like dead time.
notes.playability: The solve is reliable. solve.mjs and fail.mjs both complete, g.close() returned no errors, and the win fired at about 50 s of game time. The tray, the bench entry and the act() flow all work. Two prompt bugs hurt play: the prompt reads 'P Play test' while P powers off and wipes the soak, and a stale hover prompt shows 'F Flip the LED' through the whole hopper job and replaces 'Enter Sign off' after a pass. The PTC re-trips every 2.65 s while left on, which is noisy, although the player can still fix the chain while it cycles.
notes.clarity: The board itself reads well (arcade-teach-23): rails, wire links on the empty pads, the + and − on the LED, and the ACROSS slot wired between the rails. The reversed LED shows its red '+' on the ground side. The text load at the bench is still heavy. The card, panel ask, story, rows, toast with formula, meter and footer come to about 70 words in arcade-teach-13. The current appears three times (meter tile, bar label and panel), and the ask twice (card and panel). Formulas are printed in failure toasts. The tier copy contradicts itself: 'PLAY TEST PASSED ✓' appears alongside 'too dim', and a motor shows FULL alongside 'too dim'. 'too dim' is even used for a motor's base current. The meter's small caps (LIGHT, LED HEAT and so on) are about 9 px, which is known under DR-48.
notes.models: Not my dimension. Incidental notes: the candy blocks with real colour bands and brass end caps read clearly. The LED's unlit dome is drawn too white (tint 0.55), so the red pinball LED looks like a white LED. The TO-92 transistor shows only B and E and there is no collector. The motor is a grey can parked beside the meter with no wiring. The play-tester is still a realistic human kid (DR-60, known).
